\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluated Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA) across seven models (7B to 32B parameters), four reasoning domains, and more than 2,400 instances with three-seed replication. The Condorcet Jury Theorem provides a precise diagnostic for Self-Consistency's plateau: same-model traces produce Fleiss' $\kappa = 0.21$--$0.82$, compressing the effective ensemble size to $K_{\text{eff}} = 1.20$--$3.63$ for nominal $K = 12$. At $K_{\text{eff}} \approx 1$, additional traces carry almost no new information, and no aggregation method operating on those traces alone can escape the plateau.

Self-extracted symbolic constraints do not resolve this bottleneck. SICA gains are confined to a narrow Goldilocks zone (${\sim}$50--55\% SC accuracy), where Mistral-7B achieves $+4.90$\,pp on FOLIO ($p = 0.013$, significant in 2 of 3 seeds). Three failure modes explain the regime boundaries: confirmation bias above ${\sim}$60\% SC (Type~A), error amplification below ${\sim}$40\% ($\Delta = -2.83$\,pp, Type~C), and non-formalizable domains (Type~B). Oracle controls substituting gold FOL annotations yield $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$), proving the aggregation mechanism is sound. Self-extraction captures only 35\% of this oracle ceiling. Nine remediation strategies spanning six intervention dimensions all fail to widen the effective zone.

The multi-candidate rate $C_0$ combined with SC accuracy provides practitioners a zero-cost deployment diagnostic: when both fall outside the Goldilocks zone, SICA offers no benefit over majority voting. Closing the oracle gap requires constraint sources that are not deterministic functions of the reasoning model's own distribution: trained extractors, external provers, or multi-model pipelines.

\paragraph{Limitations.} Our evaluation is restricted to same-model self-extraction. Trained extractors and multi-model ensembles may achieve higher extraction quality and wider effective zones, but fall outside the scope of this study. The Goldilocks zone boundaries (${\sim}$50--55\%) are empirical and may shift with different model families or task distributions.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluated Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA) across seven models (7B to 32B parameters), four reasoning domains, and more than 2,400 instances with three-seed replication. The Condorcet Jury Theorem provides a precise diagnostic for Self-Consistency's plateau: same-model traces produce Fleiss' $\kappa = 0.21$--$0.82$, compressing the effective ensemble size to $K_{\text{eff}} = 1.20$--$3.63$ for nominal $K = 12$. At $K_{\text{eff}} \approx 1$, additional traces carry almost no new information, and no aggregation method operating on those traces alone can escape the plateau.

Self-extracted symbolic constraints do not resolve this bottleneck. SICA gains are confined to a narrow Goldilocks zone (${\sim}$50--55\% SC accuracy), where Mistral-7B achieves $+4.90$\,pp on FOLIO ($p = 0.013$, significant in 2 of 3 seeds). Three failure modes explain the regime boundaries: confirmation bias above ${\sim}$60\% SC (Type~A), error amplification below ${\sim}$40\% ($\Delta = -2.83$\,pp, Type~C), and non-formalizable domains (Type~B). Oracle controls substituting gold FOL annotations yield $+14.22$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$), proving the aggregation mechanism is sound. Self-extraction captures only 35\% of this oracle ceiling. Nine remediation strategies spanning six intervention dimensions all fail to widen the effective zone.

The multi-candidate rate $C_0$ combined with SC accuracy provides practitioners a zero-cost deployment diagnostic: when both fall outside the Goldilocks zone, SICA offers no benefit over majority voting. Closing the oracle gap requires constraint sources that are not deterministic functions of the reasoning model's own distribution: trained extractors, external provers, or multi-model pipelines.

\paragraph{Limitations.} Our evaluation is restricted to same-model self-extraction. Trained extractors and multi-model ensembles may achieve higher extraction quality and wider effective zones, but fall outside the scope of this study. The Goldilocks zone boundaries (${\sim}$50--55\%) are empirical and may shift with different model families or task distributions.

attachment.snippet: 1	Self-Consistency (SC) majority voting over multiple chain-of-thought traces is the dominant test-time aggregation strategy for large language models (LLMs), but accuracy gains saturate as sample count grows. The Condorcet Jury Theorem (CJT) explains this plateau: same-model traces are correlated voters, so additional samples carry diminishing independent information. Symbolic constraints expressed in first-order logic (FOL) appear to offer a way forward, since formal validity is independent of the generative model. Yet when constraints are extracted by the same model that produces the traces, they inherit the traces' correlation structure. We term this the \emph{independence bottleneck}. We study this bottleneck through Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA), which extracts FOL constraints from reasoning traces and selects answers via weighted partial MAX-SAT. Evaluating seven models (7B to 32B parameters) across four reasoning domains with over 2,400 instances and three-seed replication, we find that SICA gains are confined to a narrow accuracy regime around 50 to 55\% SC baseline. Outside this zone, constraints either echo the majority (confirmation bias) or amplify errors. Oracle controls with gold FOL annotations confirm the aggregation mechanism is sound, yet self-extraction captures only 35\% of the oracle ceiling. Nine remediation strategies spanning six intervention dimensions all fail to widen the effective zone. The bottleneck is structural: same-model self-extraction cannot supply the independent signal that CJT requires for aggregation to surpass majority voting.

attachment.snippet: 1	Self-Consistency (SC) majority voting over multiple chain-of-thought traces is the dominant test-time aggregation strategy for large language models (LLMs), but accuracy gains saturate as sample count grows. The Condorcet Jury Theorem (CJT) explains this plateau: same-model traces are correlated voters, so additional samples carry diminishing independent information. Symbolic constraints expressed in first-order logic (FOL) appear to offer a way forward, since formal validity is independent of the generative model. Yet when constraints are extracted by the same model that produces the traces, they inherit the traces' correlation structure. We term this the \emph{independence bottleneck}. We study this bottleneck through Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA), which extracts FOL constraints from reasoning traces and selects answers via weighted partial MAX-SAT. Evaluating seven models (7B to 32B parameters) across four reasoning domains with over 2,400 instances and three-seed replication, we find that SICA gains are confined to a narrow accuracy regime around 50 to 55\% SC baseline. Outside this zone, constraints either echo the majority (confirmation bias) or amplify errors. Oracle controls with gold FOL annotations confirm the aggregation mechanism is sound, yet self-extraction captures only 35\% of the oracle ceiling. Nine remediation strategies spanning six intervention dimensions all fail to widen the effective zone. The bottleneck is structural: same-model self-extraction cannot supply the independent signal that CJT requires for aggregation to surpass majority voting.

39	\label{sec:extraction-taxonomy}

41	Constraints must discriminate between candidate answers for MAX-SAT to produce a ranking different from majority vote. At the source-trace level, 39.2\% of total constraint weight originates from traces whose answer differs from the plurality, but only 12.1\% of individual constraints fall into this minority category. At the Z3 semantic level, 91.8\% of constraints [95\% CI: 91.2, 92.4] are technically discriminative, producing different satisfiability outcomes when evaluated against different candidate answers. Only 8.2\% are non-discriminative.

43	The high discriminative rate does not translate into accuracy gains because discrimination mirrors the model's own answer distribution. Each trace produces constraints with its own variable names, so Z3 treats identically-intended propositions as unrelated symbols; among cross-answer constraint pairs, 56.4\% share zero Z3 variables. This variable isolation means constraints from different traces are trivially jointly satisfiable, and MAX-SAT retains nearly all of them regardless of source answer. Removing the 8.2\% non-discriminative constraints yields zero accuracy improvement. The discriminative majority does not provide independent signal; it reinforces the majority answer that SC would already select. This confirmation bias, not a lack of discrimination, explains why SICA degenerates to majority voting (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).

\paragraph{Condorcet Jury Theorem and Ensemble Diversity.}
The Condorcet Jury Theorem (CJT) \citep{condorcet1785} establishes that majority voting among independent voters, each correct with probability $p > 0.5$, converges to correctness as the number of voters grows. \citet{austensmith1996} extend this result to information aggregation under strategic conditions. \citet{ladha1992correlated} prove that correlated voters reduce the effective ensemble size, a result we operationalize as $K_{\text{eff}} = K / (1 + (K{-}1) \cdot \kappa)$ in \S\ref{sec:condorcet}. \citet{lefort2024condorcet_llm} apply the CJT framework to LLM ensemble sentiment classification and document independence violations when all ensemble members share the same architecture. We extend this line of work to reasoning-trace aggregation, measuring $\kappa$ and $K_{\text{eff}}$ across 10 model-dataset conditions (\S\ref{sec:effective-k}). Fleiss' $\kappa$ \citep{fleiss1971kappa} serves as our inter-rater agreement metric, connecting the voting-theory framework to a concrete diagnostic for when symbolic aggregation can improve over majority voting.
